Who cancels, and how angrily? Measuring the moral content of 8.6 million tweets

NLP
text analytics
measurement validation
Python
R
HPC
Cancellation talk is more punitive than restorative everywhere, the partisan difference in outrage is real but small, and the right folds cancel culture into a wider enemy more than the left does.
Published

July 22, 2026

In brief. It seems as if almost everyone has a strong opinion about cancel culture, but witnessing “cancellations” in an algorithm-derived twitter feed likely only gives part of the picture. To understand what’s actually going on, I collected 8.6 million tweets across five contexts (discussing ‘cancel culture’ itself, the “is over party” hashtag, canceled academics, celebrities, and private citizens). From this corpus, I used lexical network analysis to infer each twitter user’s partisan lean from their bio and scored every tweet for moral and affective content with a dictionary and two transformer models, giving me the largest dataset of social media posts discussing cancel culture I’ve seen in the literature.

8.6M tweets4.0M usersTF-IDF and semantic networksMoral FoundationsRoBERTa classifiersBERTopiccluster-robust effect sizesSLURM

So what?

“Cancel culture” gets invoked in newsrooms, legislatures, and product-policy meetings with total confidence and very little measurement. The public debate has three claims baked in: that it is a left-wing practice, that it is about accountability, and that it is one thing. Each of those is testable if you treat the discourse as data. The question for anyone who moderates content, measures brand sentiment, or studies online behavior is the same one: can you measure moral condemnation at scale without fooling yourself, and what does the measurement show?

Data

NoteWhat the analysis used, and what this page can show

The analyzed corpus is 8,572,185 original English-language tweets from 4,035,488 users, collected through the Twitter Academic Research API between November 2022 and January 2023, deduplicated, with retweets removed so the unit is authored text. Platform terms prohibit redistributing tweet or bio text, so tweet content is reported only in aggregate. Everything on this page is computed from user-level or study-level aggregates; the small CSVs behind each figure are in the site repository. Analysis code is at github.com/zjschroeder/Cancel-Culture-Text-Analysis.

labels = FileAttachment("data/study_labels.csv").csv({typed: true})
studyName = new Map(labels.map(d => [d.study, d.short_label]))
corpus = [
  {study: "Cancel Culture", tweets: 3907450, users: 1690113, lens: "the #cancelculture meme"},
  {study: "Is Over Party", tweets: 1953936, users: 1069485, lens: "the \"___ is over party\" hashtag"},
  {study: "Academics", tweets: 773339, users: 325957, lens: "65 canceled faculty"},
  {study: "Celebrities", tweets: 1819005, users: 878659, lens: "12 canceled celebrities"},
  {study: "Civilians", tweets: 118455, users: 71274, lens: "7 viral racism cases"}
]
Inputs.table(corpus, {columns: ["study", "lens", "tweets", "users"], header: {study: "Sample", lens: "Lens", tweets: "Tweets", users: "Unique users"}, format: {tweets: d => d.toLocaleString(), users: d => d.toLocaleString()}, width: {study: 130, lens: 260}})

What I did

The pipeline crosses three environments. Python handled ingestion and cleaning (JSON flattening, a deliberately ordered cleaner that keeps emoji and hashtags because affect is the signal, lemmatization with a parallel stemmed branch for a sensitivity check). R and quanteda built sparse document-feature matrices and TF-IDF for tweets and bios separately, then the semantic networks. Heavy jobs, including GPU inference for the transformer classifiers, ran on the University of Oregon’s Talapas cluster through SLURM; the run guide I wrote for it became the lab’s reference.

Three measurement decisions did most of the work.

Partisan lean without asking anyone. Following Essig and DellaPosta (2024), explicit partisan terms in bios were collapsed to a liberal pole and a conservative pole, and every other bio term was scored by its cosine similarity to each pole in TF-IDF space. That gives a categorical lean for the 1 to 8% of users who state a partisan term and a continuous affiliation score for roughly half of all users. The continuous score was validated against the categorical lean and against an independent latent scaling of the same bios (r = .28 to .43 across samples).

Moral content by triangulation, not by one lexicon. Each tweet was scored with the Moral Foundations Dictionary and its crowd-sourced extension, plus MoralBERT (vice/virtue) and Mformer (foundation presence), plus TweetNLP’s RoBERTa emotion, offensive-language, hate, irony, and sentiment classifiers. The outrage measure is the point where the dictionary vice composite and the transformer vice composite agree (r = .28); a one-factor model over the three moral instruments loads positively in every sample. The anger classifier, notably, does not track moral condemnation on this corpus at all, and the page says so rather than hiding it.

Effect sizes on users, not tweets. With samples in the millions every contrast is “significant,” and tweets nest within prolific authors. All contrasts are Cohen’s d on one-row-per-author aggregates, with cluster-robust standard errors and intraclass correlations reported alongside (the design effect runs about 1.2, and the naive standard errors were 2 to 2.3 times too small).

What I found

1. Partisanship is legible in how people describe themselves, even when they never mention politics

Users who share nonpolitical bio vocabulary also tend to share partisan lean. Modularity of the liberal/conservative partition on the bio-similarity network is about 0.13 in the two largest samples, close to Essig and DellaPosta’s benchmark of 0.17, and climbs to 0.20 to 0.35 in the smaller, more sorted samples. Lemmatized and stemmed tokenizations agree, so the pattern is a property of the language rather than the preprocessing.

modularity = [
  {study: "Cancel Culture", users: 265068, lemmatized: 0.127, stemmed: 0.128},
  {study: "Is Over Party", users: 164939, lemmatized: 0.131, stemmed: 0.116},
  {study: "Academics", users: 26105, lemmatized: 0.346, stemmed: 0.275},
  {study: "Celebrities", users: 18485, lemmatized: 0.271, stemmed: 0.210},
  {study: "Civilians", users: 5300, lemmatized: 0.204, stemmed: 0.205}
]
modLong = modularity.flatMap(d => [
  {study: d.study, users: d.users, tokenization: "lemmatized", Q: d.lemmatized},
  {study: d.study, users: d.users, tokenization: "stemmed", Q: d.stemmed}
])
Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 110, height: 300, width: 720,
  x: {label: "Modularity (Newman-Girvan Q) →", domain: [0, 0.4], grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: modularity.map(d => d.study)},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["lemmatized", "stemmed"], range: ["#0b5c82", "#c98a1a"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0.17], {stroke: "#6b7280", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.text([{x: 0.17, y: "Cancel Culture"}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: ["Essig & DellaPosta benchmark, Q = 0.17"], dy: -22, dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#6b7280", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.dot(modLong, {x: "Q", y: "study", fill: "tokenization", r: 6, tip: true, title: d => `${d.study} (${d.tokenization})\nQ = ${d.Q}\n${d.users.toLocaleString()} users in network`})
  ]
})

Partisan homophily in bio language: modularity of the liberal/conservative partition, by sample and tokenization. Dashed line is the Essig and DellaPosta (2024) benchmark.

2. Conservative-leaning users run hotter on outrage and the binding foundations, but the differences are small

Moral Foundations Theory predicts that conservatives lean on loyalty, authority, and sanctity and that the “vice” poles (harm, betrayal, subversion, degradation) should show up more in punitive talk. That is the direction the data take. The size is another matter: the largest contrast is the outrage proxy at d = 0.06. I read this as directional consistency, not a substantial difference, and it still cuts against the folk “left-wing outrage” story.

es = FileAttachment("data/effect_sizes.csv").csv({typed: true})
esOrder = ["care","fairness","loyalty","authority","sanctity","harm","cheating","betrayal","subversion","degradation","outrage_proxy","moral_total","like_rate","retweet_rate","reply_rate","quote_rate"]
esLabel = new Map([["outrage_proxy","Outrage proxy (5 vices)"],["moral_total","Moral total"],["like_rate","Like rate"],["retweet_rate","Retweet rate"],["reply_rate","Reply rate"],["quote_rate","Quote rate"]])
esData = es.filter(d => esOrder.includes(d.outcome)).map(d => ({...d, label: esLabel.get(d.outcome) ?? d.outcome[0].toUpperCase() + d.outcome.slice(1), family: ["care","fairness"].includes(d.outcome) ? "individualizing" : ["loyalty","authority","sanctity"].includes(d.outcome) ? "binding" : ["harm","cheating","betrayal","subversion","degradation","outrage_proxy","moral_total"].includes(d.outcome) ? "vice / composite" : "engagement"}))
Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 150, height: 420, width: 720,
  x: {label: "Cohen's d (conservative − liberal) →", domain: [-0.04, 0.08], grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: esOrder.map(o => esLabel.get(o) ?? o[0].toUpperCase() + o.slice(1))},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["individualizing","binding","vice / composite","engagement"], range: ["#2a9d8f","#0b5c82","#c0392b","#8a8f98"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.barX(esData, {x: "cohens_d_con_minus_lib", y: "label", fill: "family", tip: true, title: d => `${d.label}\nd = ${d.cohens_d_con_minus_lib}\nM liberal = ${d.mean_liberal}, M conservative = ${d.mean_conservative}`})
  ]
})

Partisan contrast by outcome, Cohen’s d (conservative minus liberal), computed on user-level means. Positive values mean conservative-leaning users score higher.

Does it depend on how big the account is? Splitting by follower tier within the two large samples, the conservative-minus-liberal gap in outrage is present in every tier and largest among everyday accounts, not among the accounts with the biggest audiences.

tier = FileAttachment("data/moral_by_lean_tier.csv").csv({typed: true})
tierOrder = ["everyday","nano","micro","macro","mega"]
viewof tierStudy = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Cancel Culture (Study 1)", 1], ["Is Over Party (Study 2)", 2]]), {value: 1, label: "Sample"})
tierData = tier.filter(d => d.study === tierStudy && d.lean !== "Neutral")
Plot.plot({
  height: 320, width: 720, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: null, axis: null, domain: ["Liberal","Conservative"]},
  y: {label: "↑ Mean outrage proxy (per-token match rate)", grid: true, zero: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Liberal","Conservative"], range: ["#2b6cb0","#c0392b"]},
  fx: {label: "Follower tier", axis: "top", domain: tierOrder.filter(t => tierData.some(d => d.size_tier === t))},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(tierData, {fx: "size_tier", x: "lean", y: "outrage", fill: "lean", tip: true, title: d => `${d.lean}, ${d.size_tier}\noutrage = ${d.outrage}\nn = ${d.n.toLocaleString()} users`})
  ]
})

Mean outrage proxy by partisan lean and follower tier. Hover for group sizes.

3. Cancellation talk is punitive everywhere, and most punitive toward the least powerful

Splitting morally loaded tweets into a punishment logic (degrade the target) and an accountability logic (center the wronged), punishment predominates in every sample, from 54% to 63% of morally loaded tweets. The tilt is steepest for the meme and the civilian cases and shallowest for academics, which fits a power-relative reading in which the least powerful targets attract the most degrading language. The frame rule was checked against a hand-coded stratified sample.

frames = FileAttachment("data/frames_by_lean.csv").csv({typed: true})
frameData = frames.filter(d => d.lean !== "None" && d.lean !== "Neutral").map(d => ({...d, sample: studyName.get(d.study) ?? d.study}))
Plot.plot({
  height: 340, width: 720, marginLeft: 60, marginTop: 40, marginBottom: 20,
  fx: {label: null, axis: "top", domain: ["Cancel Culture","Is Over Party","Academics","Celebrities","Civilians"]},
  x: {label: null, axis: null, domain: ["Liberal","Conservative"]},
  y: {label: "↑ Punishment share of morally loaded tweets", domain: [0.4, 0.75], grid: true, tickFormat: ".0%"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Liberal","Conservative"], range: ["#2b6cb0","#c0392b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "#9ca3af", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.barY(frameData, {fx: "sample", x: "lean", y: "punishment_share", fill: "lean", tip: true, title: d => `${d.sample}, ${d.lean}\npunishment share = ${(d.punishment_share*100).toFixed(1)}%\nn = ${d.n_moral.toLocaleString()} morally loaded tweets`})
  ]
})

Share of morally loaded tweets classified under the punishment frame, by sample and author lean. Bar width is not scaled to n; hover for counts.

4. The right bundles cancel culture with a wider enemy

Phelan (2025) argues that the political right folds woke, CRT, SJW, and cancellation into one interchangeable target. If so, conservative cancellation talk should reach for that cluster vocabulary more often. It does, in every sample with enough authors to trust: in the meme sample the rate is 11.0% for conservative-leaning authors against 7.9% for liberal-leaning ones, about 39% higher. This is the finding I hold with the most confidence, because it is the most direct test of a specific prior claim.

5. Outrage arrives after the story, not with it

Anchoring each canceled academic, celebrity, and civilian to their own peak-volume day and tracing the outrage rate across a 60-day window, the moral temperature at the peak is near baseline. Outrage accumulates over the following days and crests a week or two later. The initial burst is informational; the condemnation builds behind it. Mean outrage is higher in the month after than the month before for all three target types, and it rises for 67% of celebrities, 60% of civilians, and 50% of academics.

eventTable = [
  {type: "Academics", targets: 39, pre: 0.00916, post: 0.01261, rises: "50%"},
  {type: "Celebrities", targets: 12, pre: 0.00393, post: 0.00767, rises: "67%"},
  {type: "Civilians", targets: 6, pre: 0.00925, post: 0.01200, rises: "60%"}
]
Inputs.table(eventTable, {header: {type: "Target type", targets: "Targets", pre: "Outrage, 30 days before", post: "Outrage, 30 days after", rises: "Targets where outrage rose"}})

What a team would do with this

A trust-and-safety or brand-listening team would take three things from this project before any of the substantive findings. First, a partisan or ideological signal can be recovered from self-description without asking users anything, and it should be validated against an independent measure before it is used, because the coverage jump (from 1 to 8% to about half of users) comes with a real drop in precision. Second, an outrage or toxicity measure built on one lexicon or one classifier will disagree with the next one; the defensible move is to triangulate and to report the agreement, including the instrument that misbehaves (here, the anger classifier). Third, with millions of records the reporting unit matters more than the test: aggregate to the author, report effect sizes, and cluster the standard errors, or every dashboard number will look decisive.

On the substance, the timing result is the operational one. If moral condemnation crests a week or two after a story peaks, the window for de-escalation, moderation staffing, or a brand response is after the volume spike, not during it.

Limits, and what I would do differently

The samples are keyword-filtered, so they over-represent engaged accounts and are not Twitter as a whole. The partisan effects are directionally consistent but tiny, and I would not let anyone quote them without the d. The frame classifier is rule-based and validated on a sample, not on the corpus. Out-of-sample replication (holding out authors, not tweets), cascade and diffusion tests, and a spline model of the dose-response curve are still to come. If I started again I would fix the reporting unit and the triangulation design before collecting anything, since retrofitting both cost more time than the models did.
